title: Anthropic Economic Index: Economic Primitives
abstract: The report introduces economic primitives for measuring AI use, including task complexity, human input, success, and interaction style. It compares multiple samples of Claude.ai conversations while warning that platform activity is not a representative sample of the economy.

authors: Autor, David H. and Kausik, B. N.
title: Resolving the Automation Paradox: Falling Labor Share, Rising Wages
abstract: A central socioeconomic concern about Artificial Intelligence is that it will lower wages by depressing the labor share - the fraction of economic output paid to labor. We show that declining labor share is more likely to raise wages. In a competitive economy with constant returns to scale, we prove that the wage-maximizing labor share depends only on the capital-to-labor ratio, implying a non-monotonic relationship between labor share and wages. When labor share exceeds this wage-maximizing level, further automation increases wages even while reducing labor's output share. Using data from the United States and eleven other industrialized countries, we estimate that labor share is too high in all twelve, implying that further automation should raise wages. Moreover, we find that falling labor share accounted for 16\% of U.S. real wage growth between 1954 and 2019. These wage gains notwithstanding, automation-driven shifts in labor share are likely to pose significant social and political challenges.

authors: Bueno de Mesquita, Ethan and Dziuda, Wioletta and Polborn, Mattias
title: The AGI Race and Existential Risk
abstract: Concerns about the race to artificial general intelligence often assume that competition and resources increase risk by accelerating development.We study a model in which firms allocate scarce resources between speed and safety.Speed increases a firm's chance of reaching AGI first but leaves fewer resources for safety; safety lowers doom risk but slows arrival.Fragmentation increases total speed and conditional doom risk by shifting a fixed industry resource pool toward speed.The model also identifies a critical market size: below it, firms have positive expected payoff from achieving AGI, while above it, firms race even though achieving AGI has negative expected value.More per-firm resources always accelerate expected arrival, but their effect on conditional doom risk changes sign at this cutoff.Policy affects risk by changing equilibrium incentives: consolidation, resource regulation, commitment devices, and cautious public entry can improve welfare in some environments.The results show that AGI risk depends not only on technical considerations, but also on market structure, resource constraints, and institutions that shape the equilibrium allocation between speed and safety.

authors: Davidson, Tom and Halperin, Basil and Houlden, Thomas and Korinek, Anton
title: When Does Automating AI Research Produce Explosive Growth? Feedback Loops in Innovation Networks
abstract: AI labs are increasingly using AI itself to accelerate AI research, creating a feedback loop that could lead to an intelligence explosion. We develop a general semi-endogenous growth model with an innovation network, where research and automation in one sector increase the productivity of research in other sectors, and derive a clean analytical condition under which growth becomes superexponential (``explosive''). We find that automating research can offset diminishing returns to ideas by activating two reinforcing channels: a technological feedback loop across research sectors, and an economic feedback loop in which higher output finances further research. Growth becomes explosive if the combined strength of technological and economic feedback loops overcomes diminishing returns. In a simple simulation calibrated to trends in AI progress, fully automating software research and modest (5%) automation in other sectors generates a singularity within six years. Bottlenecks do not overturn the result if task automation advances sufficiently fast.
topics: AI research automation; innovation networks; feedback loops; spectral radius; explosive growth; compute
method: Semi-endogenous innovation network represented by a nonnegative feedback matrix, with a spectral-radius classification of growth regimes.
key_results: Technological and economic feedback can jointly overcome diminishing returns and generate superexponential growth; the criterion classifies the eventual regime rather than fixing a unique transition date.
use_in_axm: Closest antecedent for the capability--compute feedback architecture, local feedback weights, scalar denominator, and explosive-growth threshold.
limits_for_axm: Its automation shares and research allocations are exogenous in the economic application. Its network theorem is not the A×M equilibrium theorem, and its simulated dates are not transferable.

title: Key Questions on Energy and AI
abstract: The report examines how artificial intelligence changes electricity demand, where data-center demand is concentrated, how AI may improve energy systems, and which infrastructure, efficiency, and policy choices determine its net energy effects.

authors: Jones, Charles I. and Tonetti, Christopher
title: Past Automation and Future A.I.: How Weak Links Tame the Growth Explosion
abstract: How much of past economic growth is due to automation, and what does this imply about the effects of A.I. in the coming decades? We perform growth accounting using a task-based model for key sectors in the U.S. economy. Historically, TFP growth is driven primarily by improvements in capital productivity. At the task level, capital productivity has grown approximately 4 percentage points per year faster than labor productivity in the U.S. private business sector, and substantially more in some industries. The main benefit of automation is therefore that we use rapidly-improving machines instead of slowly-improving humans on an increasing share of tasks. Looking to the future, we develop an endogenous growth model in which the production of both goods and ideas is endogenously automated and calibrate the model based on our historical accounting. Automation leads economic growth to accelerate, but the acceleration is remarkably slow because of the prominence of weak links, i.e., an elasticity of substitution among tasks substantially less than one. Even when most tasks are automated by rapidly-improving capital, output is constrained by the tasks performed by slowly-improving labor.
topics: automation; weak links; task model; factor shares; endogenous growth; AI; delayed takeoff
evidence_type: growth accounting, theory, and calibrated simulation
method: Task-level growth accounting plus an endogenous-growth model in which production and idea creation are progressively automated.
key_results: Weak links can make the acceleration remarkably slow even when most tasks are automated. Simulated aggregate paths can remain similar for decades before diverging; depending on the tail behavior and timing of automation, the capital share can converge to zero, one, or an interior value.
use_in_axm: Closest dynamic precedent for the long apparent plateau followed by a steep takeoff and for the fact that automation alone does not determine limiting factor shares.
limits_for_axm: Its elasticity aggregates tasks and its automation margin changes task assignment. That mechanism is not the A×M labor--AI CES, and its calendar dates cannot be imported.
notes: Working paper, Version 0.5, May 2026

title: Measuring the AI Economy
abstract: We construct a macroeconomic estimate of total AI production for the United States, combining inference and R&D/training activities and applying quality adjustments based on the evolution of API prices at fixed performance levels and the pace of algorithmic progress. We estimate that nominal AI compute spending grew over 140% per year each in 2024 and 2025, raw compute capacity grew over 200% per year, and quality-adjusted AI output grew over 2000% per year. These growth rates reflect expanding data-center capacity, continued improvements in chip efficiency, and rapid algorithmic progress.
topics: AI measurement; inference; training; research and development; compute; algorithms; model capital; satellite accounts
method: Macroeconomic measurement of inference and R&D/training, with quality adjustment for API prices, chip efficiency, and algorithmic progress.
key_results: AI activity grows much faster after quality adjustment than nominal compute spending, because hardware capacity and algorithmic efficiency compound.
use_in_axm: Provides the measurement vocabulary used to distinguish inference compute, research or training compute, algorithms, and model capital.
limits_for_axm: It does not identify the model's substitution elasticities, derive equilibrium prices or rents, or validate the simulated transition timing.

title: Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models
abstract: METR estimates the length of software, machine-learning, and cybersecurity tasks that frontier AI agents can complete with 50 percent success, where task length is measured by human-expert completion time. The public release includes model-level confidence intervals and cautions that estimates above 16 hours are unreliable with the current task suite.
notes: Updated May 8, 2026

title: Annual Report on Form 10-K for the Fiscal Year Ended January 25, 2026
abstract: NVIDIA's Form 10-K reports the company's audited financial results, business segments, risk factors, and operating discussion for the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026. For this project, the relevant evidence is the scale and growth of data-center revenue; the filing is not a measure of total AI-industry revenue.

authors: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence
title: The 2026 AI Index Report
abstract: The 2026 AI Index compiles evidence on frontier-model performance, compute capacity, costs, investment, industry structure, adoption, policy, and public attitudes. The report emphasizes the increasing scale of industry-led model development and the rapid growth of the physical and commercial infrastructure supporting AI.

title: Automation and Aging in General Equilibrium: AI Capital, Fertility, and the Return to Capital
abstract: This paper develops a general equilibrium overlapping-generations model with endogenous fertility, in which firms accumulate both physical and artificial intelligence (AI) capital, and uses it to study the macroeconomic transmission of two structural disturbances: an AI technology shock and a longevity shock. The AI shock acts as a capital-demand disturbance: it raises all rates of return, most sharply the return to AI capital, reallocates investment from physical to AI capital, and produces a front-loaded output expansion that decays monotonically. The longevity shock acts as a saving-supply disturbance: it deepens the aggregate capital stock, compresses returns and the real interest rate, and generates hump-shaped, persistent dynamics. The two shocks move fertility in opposite directions: AI raises it modestly through an income effect, while longevity lowers it by strengthening the life-cycle saving motive and the cost of childrearing. A forecast-error variance decomposition attributes most aggregate volatility to the longevity shock, while the AI shock dominates the variance of the return to AI capital. Fertility is strongly countercyclical and almost perfectly negatively correlated with hours worked, placing household time allocation at the center of the mechanism. Robustness checks across the capital share, the shock persistence, and the utility specification show that only an empirically implausible labor-AI elasticity reverses the wage and fertility signs. A welfare analysis finds the AI shock welfare-improving under complementarity, whereas longevity produces a short-run welfare loss that recedes as capital deepening raises wages, since households initially compress consumption and fertility to finance a longer retirement.

title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
abstract: SUMMARY This paper evaluates claims about the large macroeconomic implications of new advances in Artificial intelligence (AI). It starts from a task-based model of AI’s effects, working through automation and task complementarities. So long as AI’s microeconomic effects are driven by cost savings/productivity improvements at the task level, its macroeconomic consequences will be given by a version of Hulten’s theorem: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and aggregate productivity gains can be estimated by what fraction of tasks are impacted and average task-level cost savings. Using existing estimates on exposure to AI and productivity improvements at the task level, these macroeconomic effects appear non-trivial but modest – no more than a 0.66% increase in total factor productivity (TFP) over 10 years. The paper then argues that even these estimates could be exaggerated, because early evidence is from easy-to-learn tasks, whereas some of the future effects will come from hard-to-learn tasks, where there are many context-dependent factors affecting decision-making and no objective outcome measures from which to learn successful performance. Consequently, predicted TFP gains over the next 10 years are even more modest and are predicted to be less than 0.53%. I also explore AI’s wage and inequality effects. I show theoretically that even when AI improves the productivity of low-skill workers in certain tasks (without creating new tasks for them), this may increase rather than reduce inequality. Empirically, I find that AI advances are unlikely to increase inequality as much as previous automation technologies because their impact is more equally distributed across demographic groups, but there is also no evidence that AI will reduce labour income inequality. Instead, AI is predicted to widen the gap between capital and labour income. Finally, some of the new tasks created by AI may have negative social value (such as the design of algorithms for online manipulation), and I discuss how to incorporate the macroeconomic effects of new tasks that may have negative social value.

title: Anthropic Economic Index: Uneven Geographic and Enterprise AI Adoption
abstract: The report analyzes sampled Claude.ai conversations and enterprise API usage to document differences in AI adoption across tasks, regions, and organizations. Its automation taxonomy distinguishes directive interactions from feedback loops and augmentation.

title: The 2025 Cloudflare Radar Year in Review
abstract: Cloudflare's annual review summarizes changes in internet traffic, security, outages, and automated crawling during 2025. Its traffic measures count network requests and therefore should not be interpreted as measures of employment, task displacement, or economic value added.

authors: Demirer, Mert and Fradkin, Andrey and Tadelis, Nadav and Peng, Sida
title: The Emerging Market for Intelligence: Pricing, Supply, and Demand for LLMs
abstract: Using API usage data from OpenRouter and Microsoft Azure, the paper documents rapid entry by models and providers, substantial price declines, persistent price dispersion within quality tiers, and frequent turnover among market leaders. It also finds horizontal and vertical differentiation across applications, preliminary short-run price elasticities slightly above one, and increasing experimentation with multiple models even though most firms concentrate usage in a single model.

authors: Erdil, Ege and Potlogea, Andrei and Besiroglu, Tamay and Roldan, Edu and Ho, Anson and Sevilla, Jaime and Barnett, Matthew and Vrzla, Matej and Sandler, Robert
title: GATE: An Integrated Assessment Model for AI Automation
abstract: Assessing the economic impacts of artificial intelligence requires integrating insights from both computer science and economics. We present the Growth and AI Transition Endogenous model (GATE), a dynamic integrated assessment model that simulates the economic effects of AI automation. GATE combines three key ingredients that have not been brought together in previous work: (1) a compute-based model of AI development, (2) an AI automation framework, and (3) a semi-endogenous growth model featuring endogenous investment and adjustment costs. The model allows users to simulate the economic effects of the transition to advanced AI across a range of potential scenarios. GATE captures the interactions between economic variables, including investment, automation, innovation, and growth, as well as AI-related inputs such as compute and algorithms. This paper explains the model's structure and functionality, emphasizing AI development for economists and economic modeling for the AI community. The model is implemented in an interactive sandbox, enabling users to explore the impact of AI under different parameter choices and policy interventions.
topics: AI automation; compute; endogenous growth; investment; integrated assessment
method: Integrated assessment model combining compute-based AI development, automation, semi-endogenous growth, investment, and adjustment costs.
key_results: The framework jointly simulates AI development, automation, investment, innovation, and aggregate growth across alternative scenarios.
use_in_axm: Main quantitative comparator for models that integrate compute, automation, investment, and growth.
limits_for_axm: It abstracts from the decentralized price system and market structure central to the A×M paper and does not supply its analytical regime classification.

title: Artificial Intelligence in the Knowledge Economy
abstract: The paper studies how AI agents reshape hierarchical organizations built around differences in human knowledge. Compute can create either autonomous agents that solve problems independently or nonautonomous agents that assist people. These two forms of AI change organizational structure and distribute gains differently across the knowledge hierarchy.
topics: artificial intelligence; knowledge economy; compute; AI agents; organization; labor income
method: Competitive equilibrium model of knowledge hierarchies in which exogenous compute is converted into autonomous or nonautonomous AI agents.
key_results: AI autonomy changes organizational structure and the distribution of gains across human knowledge types; compute has an endogenous rental price but fixed aggregate supply.
use_in_axm: Closest precedent for treating compute as a rival input that produces scalable AI agents while preserving an explicit market price.
limits_for_axm: The model is static, has exogenous compute and zero economic profit, and does not include training or research feedback.
notes: Concise editorial synopsis of the official abstract; it is not author-written text.

title: Energy and AI
abstract: The report studies the electricity required by data centers and artificial intelligence, the geographic concentration of demand, the scope for efficiency improvements, and the ways in which AI could also transform energy production and consumption.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Research and Development
abstract: How much can AI accelerate progress in different research fields?This paper shows that three features-the share of research tasks AI performs, the productivity of AI at those tasks, and the strength of bottlenecks-are key determinants of AI's implications in any area, from cancer therapeutics to software design.The model maps changes in AI capabilities to research outcomes, quantifies the "marginal returns to intelligence," and shows how AI can shift returns to R&D investment.Concepts like superintelligence, Powerful AI, and Transformative AI are further engaged and disciplined.Finally, the framework sets a measurement agenda linking AI benchmarks to field-specific opportunities for accelerating progress.

authors: Kokotajlo, Daniel and Alexander, Scott and Larsen, Thomas and Lifland, Eli and Dean, Romeo
title: AI 2027
abstract: AI 2027 presents a scenario in which AI systems automate a growing share of AI research during 2027, rapidly produce systems with capabilities beyond those of human researchers, and create severe alignment and geopolitical risks. The scenario is a forecast exercise rather than an estimated economic model.
notes: Scenario forecast published April 3, 2025

title: Details about METR's Preliminary Evaluation of Claude 3.7
abstract: METR's preliminary evaluation tests Claude 3.7 on a five-task subset of RE-Bench. With a 32-hour budget per task, the agent matched the median score of human experts given eight hours, while METR emphasizes that the comparison is preliminary and not directly comparable with every earlier evaluation.

title: We Won't Be Missed: Work and Growth in the AGI World
abstract: This chapter explores the long-run implications of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) for economic growth and labor markets. AGI makes it feasible to perform all economically valuable work using compute. I distinguish between bottleneck and supplementary work—tasks that are essential versus non-essential for unhindered growth. As computational resources expand: (i) the economy automates all bottleneck work, (ii) some supplementary work may be left exclusively to humans, (iii) output becomes linear in compute and labor and its growth is driven by the expansion of compute, (iv) wages converge to the opportunity cost of computational resources required to reproduce human work, and (v) the share of labor income in GDP converges to zero.
topics: AGI; compute; bottleneck work; labor share; wages; economic growth
method: Long-run model in which AGI can reproduce all economically valuable bottleneck work using expanding compute.
key_results: Once compute can perform all bottleneck work, growth becomes compute-driven, wages are tied to compute's opportunity cost, and labor's income share converges to zero.
use_in_axm: Closest antecedent for the conditional limiting distribution in which the human bottleneck disappears and labor's share vanishes.
limits_for_axm: It characterizes the endpoint, not the endogenous delayed takeoff, monopoly rents, or the split between inference and research compute.

authors: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence
title: The 2025 AI Index Report
abstract: The 2025 AI Index synthesizes evidence on technical performance, investment, adoption, responsible AI, public opinion, education, and policy. It documents rapid improvements in benchmark performance and falling inference costs while emphasizing persistent limitations in reliability, transparency, and standardized evaluation.

title: Is Software Eating the World?
abstract: When explaining the declining labor income share in advanced economies, the macro literature finds that the elasticity of substitution between capital and labor is greater than one.However, the vast majority of micro-level estimates shows that capital and labor are complements (elasticity less than one).Using firm-and establishment-level data from Korea, we divide capital into equipment and software, as they may interact with labor in different ways.Our estimation shows that equipment and labor are complements (elasticity 0.6), consistent with other micro-level estimates, but software and labor are substitutes (1.6), a novel finding that helps reconcile the macro vs. micro-literature elasticity discord.As the quality of software improves, labor shares fall within firms because of factor substitution and endogenously rising markups.In addition, production reallocates toward firms that use software more intensively, as they become effectively more productive.Because in the data these firms have higher markups and lower labor shares, the reallocation further raises the aggregate markup and reduces the aggregate labor share.The rise of software accounts for two-thirds of the labor share decline in Korea between 1990 and 2018.The factor substitution and the markup channels are equally important.On the other hand, the falling equipment price plays a minor role, because the factor substitution and the markup channels offset each other.

title: Market Power in Artificial Intelligence
abstract: This paper surveys the relevant existing literature that can help researchers and policy makers understand the drivers of competition in markets that constitute the provision of artificial intelligence products.The focus is on three broad markets: training data, input data, and AI predictions.It is shown that a key factor in determining the emergence and persistence of market power will be the operation of markets for data that would allow for trading data across firm boundaries.

title: The AI Dilemma: Growth versus Existential Risk
abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they may increase economic growth as AI augments our ability to innovate. On the other hand, many experts worry that these advances entail existential risk: creating a superintelligence misaligned with human values could lead to catastrophic outcomes, even possibly human extinction. This paper considers the optimal use of AI technology in the presence of these opportunities and risks. Under what conditions should we continue the rapid progress of AI, and under what conditions should we stop? (JEL D11, D81, H43, I31, O31)

title: Concentrating Intelligence: Scaling and Market Structure in Artificial Intelligence
abstract: This paper examines the evolving structure and competition dynamics of the rapidly growing market for foundation models, with a focus on large language models (LLMs).We describe the technological characteristics that shape the AI industry and have given rise to fierce competition among the leading players.The paper analyzes the cost structure of foundation models, emphasizing the importance of key inputs such as computational resources, data, and talent, and identifies significant economies of scale and scope that may create a tendency towards greater market concentration in the future.We explore two concerns for competition, the risk of market tipping and the implications of vertical integration, and we evaluate policy remedies that aim to maintain a competitive landscape.Looking ahead to increasingly transformative AI systems, we discuss how market concentration could translate into unprecedented accumulation of power, highlighting the broader societal stakes of competition policy.
notes: Published in Economic Policy, 2025

title: Evaluating Frontier AI R&D Capabilities of Language Model Agents against Human Experts
abstract: RE-Bench compares language-model agents with human experts on machine-learning research-engineering tasks under different time budgets. In the original evaluation, humans retained a large advantage at the longest budget even though AI agents were competitive at shorter horizons.

title: Training Compute of Frontier AI Models Grows by 4--5x per Year
abstract: Epoch AI's expanded model database indicates that training compute for recent notable and frontier models grew by roughly four to five times per year between 2010 and May 2024. Similar growth appears across recent large language models and models produced by leading AI companies.

authors: Guerreiro, Joao and Rebelo, Sergio and Teles, Pedro
title: Regulating Artificial Intelligence
abstract: We consider an environment in which there is substantial uncertainty about the potential negative external effects of AI algorithms.We find that subjecting algorithm implementation to regulatory approval or mandating testing is insufficient to implement the social optimum.When testing costs are low, a combination of mandatory testing for external effects and making developers liable for the negative external effects of their algorithms comes close to implementing the social optimum even when developers have limited liability.
notes: Revised May 2026

title: Economic Growth under Transformative AI
abstract: Recent advances in AI may herald the near arrival of systems that can automate essentially all work. We review the macroeconomic implications of this scenario, in a framework synthesizing several strands of the relevant literature. Robustly, fully automating production alone (so that machines can self-replicate) would dramatically raise the growth rate and lower the labor share, breaking the Kaldor Facts that have long characterized frontier growth. Automating R&D (so that machines can self-improve) would accelerate the transformation, but may not produce it in isolation. Wages—the product of exploding output and a plummeting labor share—may rise or fall, depending on the returns to scale, the importance of natural resources, and the direction of technical change.
topics: transformative AI; production automation; research automation; growth; labor share; wages; natural resources
method: Macroeconomic framework separating automation of ordinary production from automation of research and development.
key_results: Full production automation can sharply raise growth and reduce labor's share; automating R&D accelerates the transformation, while wage effects depend on scale, resources, and technical change.
use_in_axm: Supports separating the production and research automation margins and distinguishing wage levels from labor's income share.
limits_for_axm: It does not use the A×M market structure or provide the paper's exact distributional decomposition.
notes: Revised April 2026

title: The Past and Future of Economic Growth: A Semi-Endogenous Perspective
abstract: The nonrivalry of ideas gives rise to increasing returns, a fact celebrated in Paul Romer's recent Nobel Prize. An implication is that the long-run rate of economic growth is the product of the degree of increasing returns and the growth rate of research effort; this is the essence of semi-endogenous growth theory. This review interprets past and future growth from a semi-endogenous perspective. For 50+ years, US growth has substantially exceeded its long-run rate because of rising educational attainment, declining misallocation, and rising (global) research intensity, implying that frontier growth could slow markedly in the future. Other forces push in the opposite direction. First is the prospect of “finding new Einsteins”: How many talented researchers have we missed historically because of the underdevelopment of China and India and because of barriers that discouraged women inventors? Second is the longer-term prospect that artificial intelligence could augment or even replace people as researchers. Throughout, the review highlights many opportunities for further research.
topics: semi-endogenous growth; research automation; singularity

authors: Moll, Benjamin and Rachel, Lukasz and Restrepo, Pascual
title: Uneven Growth: Automation's Impact on Income and Wealth Inequality
abstract: The benefits of new technologies accrue not only to high-skilled labor but also to owners of capital through higher capital incomes. The paper develops a tractable theory linking technology to personal income and wealth distributions and isolates a mechanism through which automation increases inequality via returns to wealth. Higher returns can coincide with stagnant wages and incomes at the bottom of the distribution.
topics: automation; wealth inequality; income inequality; returns to wealth; wages; heterogeneous households
method: Heterogeneous-household automation model linking factor returns to income and wealth distributions, with a multi-asset quantitative extension.
key_results: Automation can increase the return to wealth, raise top income and wealth concentration, and limit wage gains for workers with few assets.
use_in_axm: Clarifies why a functional decomposition of output is not enough to infer interpersonal inequality: ownership of capital and developer profit matters.
limits_for_axm: The A×M paper has a representative household and therefore does not reproduce this personal-distribution mechanism.
notes: Concise editorial synopsis of the official abstract; it is not author-written text.

title: Are We Approaching an Economic Singularity? Information Technology and the Future of Economic Growth
abstract: What are the prospects for long-run economic growth? One prominent line of economic thinking is the trend toward stagnation. Stagnationism has a long history in economics, beginning prominently with Malthus and occasionally surfacing in different guises. Prominent themes here are the following: Will economic growth slow and perhaps even reverse under the weight of resource depletion? Will overpopulation and diminishing returns lower living standards? Will unchecked CO 2 emissions lead to catastrophic changes in climate and human systems? Have we depleted the store of potential great inventions? Will the aging society lead to diminished innovativeness? (JEL D83, E25, O31, O32, O41, O47)

authors: Autor, David and Dorn, David and Katz, Lawrence F. and Patterson, Christina and Van Reenen, John
title: The Fall of the Labor Share and the Rise of Superstar Firms
abstract: The paper uses U.S. Economic Census microdata to assess whether the decline in labor's share reflects reallocation toward superstar firms. Industries in which concentration rises most exhibit larger labor-share declines, and much of the aggregate decline comes from reallocation toward large, productive firms with high markups and low labor shares rather than from an equal decline within every firm.
topics: labor share; superstar firms; concentration; markups; reallocation; productivity
method: Firm-level panel evidence on concentration, markups, productivity, and between-firm reallocation.
key_results: Aggregate labor-share declines can reflect reallocation toward high-markup, low-labor-share firms rather than only within-firm factor substitution.
use_in_axm: Provides an empirical market-structure counterpart to the model's separation of labor payments and monopoly profit.
limits_for_axm: It does not identify advanced AI, inference or research compute, or a feedback-driven growth transition.
notes: Concise editorial synopsis of the official abstract; it is not author-written text.

title: Declining Labor and Capital Shares
abstract: This paper presents direct measures of capital costs, equal to the product of the required rate of return on capital and the value of the capital stock. The capital share does not offset the decline in the labor share. Instead, a large increase in the share of pure profits offsets declines in the shares of both labor and capital. Industry data show that increases in concentration are associated with declines in the labor share.
topics: labor share; capital share; pure profits; concentration; market power; accounting
method: Direct measurement of capital costs and pure profits using U.S. national and industry accounts.
key_results: The decline in labor's share need not reappear as competitive capital income; both labor and capital shares can fall while pure profits rise.
use_in_axm: Supports separating the fixed gross capital payment from developer profit when interpreting the fall in labor's share.
limits_for_axm: The evidence concerns historical U.S. accounts and concentration, not the allocation of AI compute or the asymptotic regimes of the model.

title: Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor
abstract: We present a framework for understanding the effects of automation and other types of technological changes on labor demand, and use it to interpret changes in US employment over the recent past. At the center of our framework is the allocation of tasks to capital and labor—the task content of production. Automation, which enables capital to replace labor in tasks it was previously engaged in, shifts the task content of production against labor because of a displacement effect. As a result, automation always reduces the labor share in value added and may reduce labor demand even as it raises productivity. The effects of automation are counterbalanced by the creation of new tasks in which labor has a comparative advantage. The introduction of new tasks changes the task content of production in favor of labor because of a reinstatement effect, and always raises the labor share and labor demand. We show how the role of changes in the task content of production—due to automation and new tasks—can be inferred from industry-level data. Our empirical decomposition suggests that the slower growth of employment over the last three decades is accounted for by an acceleration in the displacement effect, especially in manufacturing, a weaker reinstatement effect, and slower growth of productivity than in previous decades.
topics: automation; new tasks; displacement; reinstatement; labor share; employment; wages
method: Task framework separating automation's displacement effect from the reinstatement effect of new human tasks, combined with an industry-level empirical decomposition.
key_results: Automation lowers labor demand and labor's share through displacement; new tasks raise both through reinstatement.
use_in_axm: Establishes the general distributional mechanism that the A×M paper takes as known rather than claiming as new.
limits_for_axm: It does not model AI-research feedback, rival inference and research compute, monopoly pricing, or delayed explosive growth.

authors: Aghion, Philippe and Jones, Benjamin F. and Jones, Charles I.
title: Artificial Intelligence and Economic Growth
venue: The Economics of Artificial Intelligence: An Agenda
abstract: This paper examines the potential impact of artificial intelligence (A.I.) on economic growth. We model A.I. as the latest form of automation, a broader process dating back more than 200 years. Electricity, internal combustion engines, and semiconductors facilitated automation in the last century, but A.I. now seems poised to automate many tasks once thought to be out of reach, from driving cars to making medical recommendations and beyond. How will this affect economic growth and the division of income between labor and capital? What about the potential emergence of singularities and superintelligence? How will the linkages between A.I. and growth be mediated by firm-level considerations, including organization and market structure? The goal throughout is to refine a set of critical questions about A.I. and economic growth and to contribute to shaping an agenda for the field. One theme that emerges is based on Baumol's cost disease insight: growth may be constrained not by what we are good at but rather by what is essential and yet hard to improve.
topics: artificial intelligence; automation; economic growth; bottlenecks; Baumol cost disease; singularity
method: Task-automation extensions of growth models, including automation in goods and idea production and essential-task bottlenecks.
key_results: Automation can raise growth sharply, but essential tasks that remain difficult to automate can bind aggregate growth for a prolonged period.
use_in_axm: Early antecedent for the claim that bottlenecks can keep aggregate growth modest even while automation advances.
limits_for_axm: The numerical automation path is exogenous, so it is not the closest precedent for the endogenous timing of the A×M takeoff.

title: The Race between Man and Machine: Implications of Technology for Growth, Factor Shares, and Employment
abstract: We examine the concerns that new technologies will render labor redundant in a framework in which tasks previously performed by labor can be automated and new versions of existing tasks, in which labor has a comparative advantage, can be created. In a static version where capital is fixed and technology is exogenous, automation reduces employment and the labor share, and may even reduce wages, while the creation of new tasks has the opposite effects. Our full model endogenizes capital accumulation and the direction of research toward automation and the creation of new tasks. If the long-run rental rate of capital relative to the wage is sufficiently low, the long-run equilibrium involves automation of all tasks. Otherwise, there exists a stable balanced growth path in which the two types of innovations go hand-in-hand.
topics: automation; tasks; labor share; wages; factor shares; endogenous growth
method: Task-based growth model with endogenous capital accumulation and directed innovation toward automation or new human tasks.
key_results: Automation displaces labor and lowers its income share; new human tasks generate a reinstatement force. Depending on relative factor costs, the long run can feature full automation or a stable balanced-growth path with both types of innovation.
use_in_axm: Canonical antecedent for the displacement--reinstatement mechanism and for the possibility that wages and labor's share move differently.
limits_for_axm: It does not separate inference from research compute, model monopoly rents, or characterize the delayed feedback-driven takeoff studied in the A×M paper.
notes: Excerpt from the official author abstract; the omitted closing sentences discuss stability and inequality with heterogeneous skills.

title: Accounting for Factorless Income
abstract: Comparing U.S. GDP with measured labor payments and imputed capital rental payments leaves a large and volatile residual, which the paper calls factorless income. It evaluates three interpretations of that residual: economic profits, unmeasured capital, or deviations of the rental rate from standard measures. The preferred interpretation materially changes measured factor shares, technology growth, and functional inequality.
topics: factorless income; profits; unmeasured capital; rental rate; factor shares; accounting
method: National-accounts decomposition under alternative interpretations of output not assigned to measured labor or imputed capital services.
key_results: The inferred distribution and technology depend critically on whether the residual is treated as profit, unmeasured capital, or a rental-rate wedge.
use_in_axm: Motivates explicit accounting of capital payments, compute resource uses, wages, and developer profit instead of assigning the residual mechanically to capital or rents.
limits_for_axm: It is an accounting exercise, not a model of AI services, research feedback, or endogenous takeoff.
notes: Concise editorial synopsis of the official abstract; it is not author-written text.

authors: Korinek, Anton and Stiglitz, Joseph E.
title: Artificial Intelligence and Its Implications for Income Distribution and Unemployment
abstract: Inequality is one of the main challenges posed by the proliferation of artificial intelligence and other forms of worker-replacing technological progress. The paper distinguishes two main distributional channels: surplus accruing to innovators and redistribution arising from factor-price changes. It also studies policy responses and the channels through which technological progress may produce technological unemployment, including in a singularity where machines dominate human labor.
topics: artificial intelligence; income distribution; innovator surplus; factor prices; unemployment; policy
method: Taxonomy and a set of stylized models of worker-replacing technical change, factor-price redistribution, innovator surplus, and policy.
key_results: AI can redistribute income both through factor prices and through rents captured by innovators; those channels require different policy responses.
use_in_axm: Supports the distinction between redistribution through factor prices and surplus captured by the innovator.
limits_for_axm: It does not provide the A×M technology, the two substitution thresholds, or the numerical delayed-takeoff transition.
notes: Concise editorial synopsis of the official abstract; it is not author-written text.

title: The Global Decline of the Labor Share
abstract: Abstract The stability of the labor share of income is a key foundation in macroeconomic models. We document, however, that the global labor share has significantly declined since the early 1980s, with the decline occurring within the large majority of countries and industries. We show that the decrease in the relative price of investment goods, often attributed to advances in information technology and the computer age, induced firms to shift away from labor and toward capital. The lower price of investment goods explains roughly half of the observed decline in the labor share, even when we allow for other mechanisms influencing factor shares, such as increasing profits, capital-augmenting technology growth, and the changing skill composition of the labor force. We highlight the implications of this explanation for welfare and macroeconomic dynamics.
topics: labor share; capital price; CES production; substitution elasticity; investment goods
method: CES capital--labor framework and cross-country evidence linking the relative price of investment to labor-share movements.
key_results: When capital and labor are gross substitutes, a lower relative price of investment can shift production toward capital and reduce labor's share.
use_in_axm: Provides the classic CES benchmark for why the location of an elasticity relative to one can change factor-share dynamics.
limits_for_axm: Its elasticity is between aggregate capital and labor, not between labor and quality-adjusted AI services; the two parameters are not empirically interchangeable.

title: A Cross-Country Empirical Investigation of the Aggregate Production Function Specification
abstract: Using a panel of 82 countries over 28 years, the paper estimates an aggregate CES production function and rejects Cobb-Douglas for the full sample. It finds greater capital-labor substitutability among richer countries and lower substitutability among poorer countries, while emphasizing that substitution above one does not by itself guarantee endogenous growth.

authors: Krusell, Per and Ohanian, Lee E. and Ríos-Rull, José-Víctor and Violante, Giovanni L.
title: Capital-Skill Complementarity and Inequality: A Macroeconomic Analysis
abstract: The paper estimates a macroeconomic production structure with capital-skill complementarity. Structures capital enters an outer production layer, while equipment capital is combined with skilled and unskilled labor in nested CES composites; changes in observed inputs account for much of the movement in the U.S. skill premium.
notes: This editorial synopsis emphasizes the production structure relevant for the capital-deepening benchmark.

title: R&D-Based Models of Economic Growth
abstract: This paper argues that the "scale effects" prediction of many recent R & D-based models of growth is inconsistent with the time-series evidence from industrialized economies. A modified version of the Romer model that is consistent with this evidence is proposed, but the extended model alters a key implication usually found in endogenous growth theory. Although growth in the extended model is generated endogenously through R & D, the long-run growth rate depends only on parameters that are usually taken to be exogenous, including the rate of population growth.

title: Population Growth and Technological Change: One Million B.C. to 1990
abstract: The nonrivalry of technology, as modeled in the endogenous growth Uterature, implies that high population spurs technological change. This paper constructs and empirically tests a model of long-run world population growth combining this implication with the Malthusian assumption that technology limits population. The model predicts that over most of history, the growth rate of population will be proportional to its level. Empirical tests support this prediction and show that historically, among societies with no possibility for technological contact, those with larger initial populations have had faster technological change and population growth.
topics: population growth; technological change; long-run growth; hyperbolic dynamics

title: The Coming Technological Singularity: How to Survive in the Post-Human Era
venue: Vision 21: Interdisciplinary Science and Engineering in the Era of Cyberspace
abstract: The paper argues that technology may soon create intelligence greater than the human level and examines whether that transition can be avoided or guided so that humanity survives.
topics: technological singularity; superhuman intelligence; AI forecasting

title: A Model of Growth through Creative Destruction
abstract: This paper develops a model based on Schumpeter's process of creative destruction. It departs from existing models of endogenous growth in emphasizing obsolescence of old technologies induced by the accumulation of knowledge and the resulting process or industrial innovations. This has both positive and normative implications for growth. In positive terms, the prospect of a high level of research in the future can deter research today by threatening the fruits of that research with rapid obsolescence. In normative terms, obsolescence creates a negative externality from innovations, and hence a tendency for laissez-faire economies to generate too many innovations, i.e too much growth. This business-stealing effect is partly compensated by the fact that innovations tend to be too small under laissez-faire. The model possesses a unique balanced growth equilibrium in which the log of GNP follows a random walk with drift. The size of the drift is the average growth rate of the economy and it is endogenous to the model ; in particular it depends on the size and likelihood of innovations resulting from research and also on the degree of market power available to an innovator.

title: Long-Run Policy Analysis and Long-Run Growth
abstract: The paper describes endogenous-growth models in which policy differences can generate persistent cross-country differences in growth rates. Growth is possible without increasing returns because a core of accumulable capital goods can be produced without direct or indirect use of nonaccumulable factors.

authors: Jones, Larry E. and Manuelli, Rodolfo E.
title: A Convex Model of Equilibrium Growth: Theory and Policy Implications
abstract: The paper develops a convex equilibrium-growth model with fixed factors in which the marginal product of capital need not converge to zero. It provides existence and characterization results and shows how tastes, technology, taxation, and trade can affect long-run growth.

title: Endogenous Technological Change
abstract: Growth in this model is driven by technological change that arises from intentional investment decisions made by profit-maximizing agents. The distinguishing feature of the technology as an input is that it is neither a conventional good nor a public good; it is a nonrival, partially excludable good. Because of the nonconvexity introduced by a nonrival good, price-taking competition cannot be supported. Instead, the equilibrium is one with monopolistic competition. The main conclusions are that the stock of human capital determines the rate of growth, that too little human capital is devoted to research in equilibrium, that integration into world markets will increase growth rates, and that having a large population is not sufficient to generate growth.

title: Moral Hazard and Observability
abstract: The paper develops a principal-agent model in which effort is not directly observable and shows how informative performance signals shape optimal incentive contracts. It establishes the informativeness principle and clarifies why imperfect monitoring creates a tradeoff between insurance and incentives.

title: A Class of Variable Elasticity of Substitution Production Functions
abstract: The paper introduces a class of production functions in which the elasticity of substitution varies with input proportions or scale, nesting familiar constant-elasticity cases under parameter restrictions.
topics: variable elasticity of substitution; production functions; VES

authors: Sato, Ryuzo and Hoffman, Ronald F.
title: Production Functions with Variable Elasticities of Factor Substitution: Some Analysis and Testing
abstract: The paper analyzes production functions whose elasticity of factor substitution is not constant and studies how those specifications can be taken to the data.

title: Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine
abstract: Good argues that a machine able to design better machines could initiate an intelligence explosion. The chapter surveys questions surrounding the construction, embodiment, learning, and control of such a system.
topics: intelligence explosion; recursive self-improvement; superintelligence
notes: No conventional abstract was available in the metadata consulted. This is an editorial synopsis. Some databases date the volume 1966; the chapter is conventionally cited as 1965.

title: Growth and the Elasticity of Factor Substitution
abstract: The paper replaces Cobb-Douglas production in the Swan growth model with a constant-elasticity technology and characterizes how factor substitution changes capital accumulation, income growth, and the relation between growth and the saving rate.
notes: No conventional abstract was available on the publisher page; this is an editorial synopsis.

authors: von Foerster, Heinz and Mora, Patricia M. and Amiot, Lawrence W.
title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026
abstract: The authors fit a hyperbolic law to historical world population data and extrapolate a finite date at which the fitted population path diverges. The exercise is an antecedent of mathematical finite-time singularity models, not a forecast supported by later demographic evidence.
topics: population; finite-time singularity; hyperbolic growth
notes: PubMed explicitly reports that no abstract is available; this is an editorial synopsis.

title: A Contribution to the Theory of Economic Growth
abstract: The paper develops a neoclassical growth model in which flexible factor substitution replaces the fixed-coefficient technology of Harrod and Domar. Its examples show how saving, population growth, and the shape of the production function determine whether capital intensity converges or continues to rise.
notes: The publisher page provides an article outline rather than a conventional abstract; this is an editorial synopsis.
